lead: Steam tables and the Mollier chart are lookup tools. The tables list measured specific volume v (m³/kg), enthalpy h (kJ/kg) and entropy s (kJ/kg·K) for water and steam, arranged by pressure or by temperature. The Mollier chart draws the same data on an h–s plane. Boiler designers and turbine testers use both to find every property from a known pair.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for the five states of a pure substance, 5.4 for hf, hfg and dryness fraction, and gauge versus absolute pressure from the basic concepts of thermodynamics.

sections.h3: What the tables hold, and which pressure to use

blocks.text: A steam table lists measured properties of water and steam, because no single simple equation covers compressed liquid, wet steam and superheated steam. Each row gives v in m³/kg, h in kJ/kg and s in kJ/kg·K.

Tables use absolute pressure. Absolute pressure is gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure; atmospheric pressure is about 1.013 bar. A boiler gauge showing 10 bar means about 11.01 bar absolute, and 11 bar is what you look up.
p<sub>abs</sub> is absolute pressure, p<sub>gauge</sub> the gauge reading, p<sub>atm</sub> the local atmospheric pressure (1.013 bar at sea level); all three in the same unit, bar or kPa.

The saturated table lists pressure with T<sub>sat</sub> or temperature with p<sub>sat</sub>. Both carry v<sub>f</sub>, v<sub>g</sub>, h<sub>f</sub>, h<sub>fg</sub>, h<sub>g</sub>, s<sub>f</sub>, s<sub>fg</sub>, s<sub>g</sub>. Subscript f marks saturated liquid, g saturated vapour, fg the change during boiling. So h<sub>g</sub> = h<sub>f</sub> + h<sub>fg</sub> and s<sub>fg</sub> = h<sub>fg</sub> / T<sub>sat</sub>, with T<sub>sat</sub> in kelvin.

Inside the dome, pressure and temperature are not independent, so a table row alone cannot fix the state. The dryness fraction x does, through the mixture rules of 5.4: h = hf + x hfg, and the same for v and s.

Above T<sub>sat</sub> the steam is superheated and the saturated table stops helping. The superheated table puts pressure down the rows and temperature across the columns. It has entries only where T is above T<sub>sat</sub> at that pressure. Each cell gives v, h and s for that (p, T).

items: Look up T<sub>sat</sub> at the given absolute pressure in the saturated table.
If T > T<sub>sat</sub>, the state is superheated; open the superheated table.
If T = T<sub>sat</sub>, the steam is saturated; use the saturated row with x.
If T < T<sub>sat</sub>, the water is a compressed liquid; use the compressed liquid table, or h ≈ h<sub>f</sub> at that temperature when pressure is small.
Find the pressure row, then the temperature column, and read v, h and s.

blocks.text: Printed tables jump in steps, often 50 K, so a given temperature may fall between two columns. Linear interpolation is accurate enough because each property varies smoothly with T at constant pressure.

blocks.where: y is the property wanted (h, v or s); (T₁, y₁) and (T₂, y₂) are the two table entries either side; T is the given temperature in °C.

blocks.text: The Mollier chart, also called the h-s diagram, plots enthalpy h in kJ/kg upward and entropy s in kJ/kg·K across. A state is one point and a process is a line, so you read with a ruler instead of a table.
The saturation dome sits in the middle. The left curve is saturated liquid (x = 0), the right curve is saturated vapour (x = 1), and they meet at the critical point near 221 bar and 374 °C.

items: Constant-pressure lines: straight inside the dome, where they are also isotherms, because at constant p the slope dh/ds equals T. In superheated steam they curve upward and steepen.
Constant-temperature lines: in superheated steam they bend towards the horizontal at low pressure, where steam behaves like an ideal gas and h depends on T alone.
Constant-dryness lines: curves for x = 0.9, 0.95 and so on inside the dome; they place a wet state without a table.

blocks.text: Reading a point on a printed chart by eye is less precise than the table: expect an error of several kJ/kg. That is fine for a sketch or a quick check of an expansion; give final exam answers from the tables. Figure 5.5.1 draws the worked expansion on the chart.

spec.aria: Enthalpy against entropy for steam. The saturated vapour line curves across the middle, the 10 bar and 1 bar lines rise to the right, and a vertical arrow at s equal to 6.93 drops from 2943.1 to 2513.7 kilojoules per kilogram.

examples.question: Steam flows at 10 bar absolute and 280 °C. (a) State whether it is superheated, saturated or compressed liquid. (b) The superheated table for 10 bar gives h = 2943.1 kJ/kg, v = 0.2327 m³/kg, s = 6.9265 kJ/kg·K at 250 °C, and h = 3051.6 kJ/kg, v = 0.2580 m³/kg, s = 7.1246 kJ/kg·K at 300 °C. Find h, v and s at 280 °C by interpolation.
steps: At 10 bar, T<sub>sat</sub> = 179.9 °C. Given T = 280 °C > 179.9 °C, so the steam is superheated by 100.1 K; the saturated table cannot give h, v or s.
Check: h<sub>g</sub> at 10 bar is 2777.1 kJ/kg; 3008.2 is larger, as superheated steam must be. Tables with a 280 °C entry give 3008.6 kJ/kg, so linear interpolation is off by only 0.4 kJ/kg.
examples.answer: Superheated steam: h ≈ 3008.2 kJ/kg, v ≈ 0.2479 m³/kg, s ≈ 7.0454 kJ/kg·K.

examples.question: Steam at 10 bar and 250 °C (h₁ = 2943.1 kJ/kg, s₁ = 6.9265 kJ/kg·K) expands isentropically in a turbine to 1 bar. At 1 bar: h<sub>f</sub> = 417.5 kJ/kg, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2257.4 kJ/kg, s<sub>f</sub> = 1.3028 kJ/kg·K, s<sub>fg</sub> = 6.0561 kJ/kg·K, s<sub>g</sub> = 7.3589 kJ/kg·K. Find the dryness fraction and enthalpy after expansion, and the drop in enthalpy.
steps: Isentropic means s₂ = s₁ = 6.9265 kJ/kg·K. On the Mollier chart this is a vertical line down from the starting point.
Compare with s<sub>g</sub> at 1 bar: 6.9265 < 7.3589, so the end state lies inside the dome: wet steam.
Enthalpy drop: h₁ − h₂ = 2943.1 − 2513.7 = 429.4 kJ/kg. This is the ideal work per kg of steam in the turbine.
Chart check: the vertical line from (s = 6.93, h = 2943) meets the 1 bar line just above the x = 0.92 curve, near h = 2514 kJ/kg, which agrees.
examples.answer: x₂ = 0.929, h₂ = 2513.7 kJ/kg, and the isentropic enthalpy drop is 429.4 kJ/kg.

traps: Entering the gauge pressure. At 10 bar gauge, absolute pressure is about 11.01 bar; properties read at 10 bar are wrong.
Using the saturated row when T > T<sub>sat</sub>. At 10 bar and 280 °C, the saturated table gives h<sub>g</sub> = 2777.1 kJ/kg, not 3008.2 kJ/kg.
Interpolating across T<sub>sat</sub>, or writing the two temperatures in the wrong order so the correction changes sign.
Giving a chart reading as a final answer to four figures. A by-eye reading carries an error of several kJ/kg, so use the tables for final values and the chart for checks and for drawing the process.

quiz.q: In a saturated steam table, what do the subscripts f, g and fg mean? Write the relation linking h<sub>f</sub>, h<sub>fg</sub> and h<sub>g</sub>.
quiz.a: f = saturated liquid, g = saturated vapour, fg = change during boiling. h<sub>g</sub> = h<sub>f</sub> + h<sub>fg</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does the superheated table have no entry for steam at 10 bar and 150 °C?
quiz.a: T<sub>sat</sub> at 10 bar is 179.9 °C, so 150 °C lies below saturation. The water is a compressed liquid there, and superheated entries begin only above T<sub>sat</sub>.

quiz.q: On an h-s chart, explain why a constant-pressure line inside the dome is also a constant-temperature line.
quiz.a: Inside the dome pressure and temperature are tied by saturation, so fixing p fixes T at T<sub>sat</sub>. The slope dh/ds at constant p equals T, which is constant, so the line is straight.

quiz.q: Steam at 5 bar absolute has x = 0.9. Given h<sub>f</sub> = 640.1 kJ/kg, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2107.4 kJ/kg and v<sub>g</sub> = 0.3749 m³/kg, find h and v.
quiz.a: h = 640.1 + 0.9 × 2107.4 = 640.1 + 1896.66 = 2536.8 kJ/kg. v ≈ x·v<sub>g</sub> = 0.9 × 0.3749 = 0.3374 m³/kg, since v<sub>f</sub> is far smaller than v<sub>g</sub>.

quiz.q: Steam at 10 bar has s = 6.0000 kJ/kg·K. Using s<sub>f</sub> = 2.1381 and s<sub>fg</sub> = 4.4469 kJ/kg·K at 10 bar, find the dryness fraction.
A student reads the Mollier chart at 10 bar and 250 °C and gets h = 2890 kJ/kg, while the table gives 2943.1 kJ/kg. Which value should be trusted, and what could explain the gap?
quiz.a: Trust the table. The gap is 53 kJ/kg, about 1.8 per cent, far more than a careful chart reading misses by. It points to a misread line: following the 225 °C isotherm instead of 250 °C at 10 bar gives about 2887 kJ/kg, almost the student’s value. A wrong isobar is the other common slip; at 15 bar and 250 °C h is 2924 kJ/kg.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial steam properties now come from the IAPWS-IF97 formulation, equations fitted to laboratory data that software such as CoolProp evaluates directly. Search "IAPWS-IF97 steam tables" to see the equations behind the printed rows.
